content.title: About
content.content: Sprouted wheat bread is a whole‑grain loaf made from wheat kernels that have been allowed to germinate. Sprouting boosts the levels of vitamins, minerals and enzymes, making the bread more nutritious and easier to digest. It has a soft crumb, a subtle nutty aroma and a golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sprouted grains contain 2–3 times more B‑vitamins than raw grains.
Antioxidant levels, such as phenolic compounds, increase during sprouting.
This bread is popular in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern diets for its digestibility.
Sprouting reduces phytic acid, improving mineral absorption.
Traditional recipes date back centuries in regions around the Mediterranean Sea.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Sprouted wheat provides higher amounts of B1, B2, B3, as well as magnesium, zinc and iron compared with regular wheat.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Enzymes formed during sprouting help break down starches and proteins more efficiently.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: The slower release of carbohydrates leads to a milder rise in blood sugar.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Both soluble and insoluble fiber promote healthy gut function and increase satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Phenolics and vitamin E protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease may react to this bread.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Sprouted wheat bread still contains gluten and is not suitable for a gluten‑free diet.

items.title: Shelf‑life
items.content: Higher moisture can cause faster spoilage; proper storage is essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sprouted wheat bread works well toasted, as a sandwich base, alongside soups, or crumbled into salads. It can be grilled, used for breadcrumbs, or paired with spreads and cheeses.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the loaf in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate in an airtight container for up to a week or freeze in portions.
